As someone who works in the field about to step in front of the downvoat "psychology is pseudoscience" freight train, I'd like to correct some of your assertions. 1) the DSM is updated every few years, as is the ICD, which is its medical counterpart (and nobody argues that medicine isn't scientific). The DSM describes symptoms as a guide for what might work or not to help that person, the same way the ICD tells you not to give a diabetic sugar pills. It's not meant to be a label, even if people misunderstand it as such due to mental health stigma. 2) Modern psychologists are required to have a doctorate, unless they were Master's level clinicians that have been practicing since the mid-80s and were "grandfathered in" to be allowed to continue to use that term. There is not one psychologist with a Bachelor's degree. 3) Psychoanalysis (Freud and Jung) has been falling out of favor for the past 50 years at least and modern therapies such as CBT, DBT, and EMDR are manualized and well-backed by research to be effective in treating most mental illness. 4) Psychology, does not recognize these "86 types of gender identification". The DSM-5 lists ONE diagnosis that relates to gender identification: Gender Dysphoria. The field of psychology has a lot of shortcomings, but it's also one of the youngest of all the sciences. Medicine was still using leeches to drain the "bad blood" in sick people thousands of years after its inception. Neurology can help us better understand the brain to make medication more effective, but considering that the human brain is the most complex thing on the face of the planet I would cut everyone a little slack.

Therapist of 7 years here. Unfortunately, it's a combination of a lot of the things you mentioned. First, the common symptom of every mental health diagnosis is that it causes distress or problems in your life. For example, if you're perfectly happy thinking suicidal thoughts all day, then you don't meet the criteria for any diagnosis, even depression, and there is no reason you would seek help anyway. I believe this is part of why homosexuality was removed as a diagnosis - outside of the push for its removal as a civil rights cause, it was also because the distress in this case was likely secondary to the social stigma around homosexuality itself, and as more people accepted it then less homosexual people were distressed by their own sexuality. Basically, if being gay doesn't bother you, then why would you need treatment?

Transgenderism is a much touchier situation in the psychology field. Psychology sees it's failure with homosexuality and appears to be erring on the side of caution this time around. The newest diagnosis is Gender Dysphoria, which is supposed to cover all bases in terms of how people 'identify'. The difference here is that these people are obviously in distress every day, every time they look in a mirror, and they are a very high suicide risk. The difficult part for researchers and clinicians is how similar this is to other recognized delusional disorders; for example, individuals suffering with Body Dysmorphic Disorder sometimes want healthy parts of their body removed because they believe them to be deformed or abnormal. Some people suffering with Schizophrenia also often claim to be other people, even individuals of the opposite sex. I'm not stating that Gender Dysmorphia or transgenderism is a set of delusional beliefs, but I think there needs to be a paradigm shift when the field is considering someone who wants their arm amputated to be delusional, but someone who wants their penis amputated to be goal-oriented. But that's just my personal opinion - the mindset of those in the field is not to challenge these beliefs. Again, if they've come to the point that they've made up their mind and actually want to go under the knife to "fix" themselves and they're ok with that decision, are they really in distress? Outcome studies for individuals who have received sexual reassignment surgery have also been mixed, further muddying up the situation. Transgenderism and sexual reassignment are generally newer cultural developments, so much more research is needed, because at the end of the day, right now psychology as a whole is failing these individuals.

Technology definitely needs to improve. Remember, we have only been able to see the physical structures of the brain (within a live individual) and measure brain activity for the past 30-40 or so years, with the fMRI being invented in 1990. If you thought the Human Genome project was an incredible undertaking, try mapping the trillions and trillions of synapses in the human brain, both in what they do individually and what they do in combination to a person's mind. Neuropsych has a long way to go.

Finally, to your point on pedophilia, I guess it could be best answered with a question. Is there any way that I or anyone else could get you to change who you are attracted to? Short answer is no, not even with Clockwork Orange-type extreme behavioral techniques (not saying we use those). This is why religious "gay conversion counseling" only made people even more distressed. It's also why, unfortunately, there are few effective interventions for those with pedophilia. To my understanding, at this point the purpose of counseling for those with pedophilia is to work on strategies that will lessen the likelihood that they act on those impulses and harm a child. This is what also makes it distinct from other "sexualities" (if you want to be so bold as to call it one), is that there is virtually no way to act on such urges that does not in some way cause non-consensual harm. So this is more a behavioral management strategy.

I'm a physician who treats a lot of transgender patients. I've read pretty much all of the major research articles in the transgender literature. With the possible exception of Meyer and Reter (1979) which was thoroughly debunked (and wasn't even a negative study - it was just equivocal), there are no studies that I know of that demonstrate overall negative outcomes. Certainly the literature is limited in that it is often underpowered (because of the rarity of the disease) and because you can't exactly do a double blind study unless you could convince the patients to wear a cone of shame like you put on a dog for a year or two after surgery. However multiple albeit limited positive studies all showing some benefit (and with decreases in suicidality that are substantially beneficial) doesn't amount to 'mixed' results.
